title: How to estimate floss quantity for a cross-stitch project
subtitle: Working out how much thread you need before you start
excerpt: Estimating floss quantity before starting a project prevents running out of a dye lot mid-work, which can leave a visible colour difference in the finished piece. The estimate is based on the number of stitches in each colour, the number of strands used, and the average thread length consumed per stitch.
sourceNotes: Floss quantity estimation for cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.
aliases: how much floss for a project

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch, sold in 8 m skeins.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: quantity before a project starts ensures you buy all the thread from the same dye lot in one purchase. A skein of DMC floss holds approximately 8 m of thread. A cross-stitch over one square of 14-count
on two strands uses approximately 3 cm of thread per stitch when wastage from starting and ending lengths is included.

Count the number of stitches in each colour. Many commercial charts include a colour stitch count in the key. If not, count each colour's filled squares manually on the chart, or use a design software tool to count for you.

Apply the rule of thumb: for 2-strand work on 14-count Aida, allow 3 cm of floss per stitch. Multiply the stitch count by 3 cm to get the total centimetres needed per colour. For 3-strand work, multiply by 4.5 cm.

Convert to skeins: divide the total centimetres by 800 cm (the 8 m per skein, expressed in cm). Round up to the nearest whole skein. For a colour with 500 stitches at 2 strands: 500 × 3 = 1,500 cm ÷ 800 = 1.875, so you need 2 skeins.

Add a buffer of one extra skein for any colour that needs more than 3 skeins, or for the main background colour if the design has a heavily stitched background. A large background area uses thread faster than scattered fill stitches.

Buy all skeins of a colour at the same time from the same supplier where possible. The lot number is printed on the paper band around each skein. Skeins from the same dye lot are a reliable match; skeins from different lots may show a slight colour variation when worked side by side.

items.symptom: You ran out of a colour before the design was finished
items.cause: The stitch count was underestimated, or the buffer skein was not purchased.
items.fix: Always buy one extra skein of any colour used in more than a small area. If you do run out, search for the same colour number from the same supplier and check the lot number before buying; if the lot is different, buy two or three extra skeins and blend threads from the old and new lots by alternating needles to minimise the visible join line.

items.symptom: Two skeins of the same colour number look slightly different
items.cause: They are from different dye lots.
items.fix: Do not use all of one skein before starting the second. Work with two needles, alternating between the two skeins every few stitches to blend the lots across the transition zone. The eye reads the blended section as a smooth transition rather than an abrupt colour change.

content.text: For a small first project (under 100 stitches per colour), the stitch count estimate is straightforward and the quantities are small. For larger projects, writing down the estimated skeins per colour alongside the thread number before purchasing keeps the purchase organised and catches any colours missed in the count.
